h1: North Carolina HOA Records Request Letter Generator
metaTitle: North Carolina HOA Records Request Letter | $19
metaDescription: Request your North Carolina HOA's records. Generate a letter citing N.C.G.S. § 47F-3-118 asking for financial and meeting records. $19.
statuteCitation: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 47F-3-118 (Planned Community Act) and § 47C-3-118 (Condominium Act)
deadline: "Reasonably available" under G.S. 47F-3-118(a); nonprofit-corporation records demands under G.S. 55A-16-02 need five business days' written notice

introParagraph: If you own property in a North Carolina planned community or condominium, you have a statutory right to inspect your association's records. The North Carolina Planned Community Act and Condominium Act both require associations to keep financial records and to make financial and other records, including records of meetings, reasonably available for examination by owners. When boards stonewall or lose paperwork, owners often have no choice but to send a formal demand letter citing the specific statute. A well-drafted records request letter puts the HOA on notice, creates a paper trail for litigation, and frequently produces documents within days. This page explains North Carolina's records access laws and helps you generate a compliant demand letter.
lawExplanation:
North Carolina governs HOA records access through two parallel statutes. The Planned Community Act (Chapter 47F) applies to planned communities created on or after January 1, 1999 (with the records provision, § 47F-3-118, also applying to earlier communities), while the Condominium Act (Chapter 47C) applies to condominiums created after October 1, 1986 (and § 47C-3-118 applies to earlier condominiums for later events). Both contain nearly identical record-keeping requirements at § 47F-3-118 and § 47C-3-118.

Under § 47F-3-118(a), the association must keep financial records sufficiently detailed to enable it to comply with the Act, and all financial and other records, including records of meetings of the association and executive board, must be made reasonably available for examination by any lot owner and the owner's authorized agents as required in the bylaws and Chapter 55A of the General Statutes. The association must also make an annual income and expense statement and balance sheet available to all lot owners at no charge within 75 days after the close of the fiscal year. Because most associations are nonprofit corporations, Chapter 55A adds records rights: under G.S. 55A-16-01 a nonprofit must keep minutes of member and board meetings as permanent records, maintain accounting records, and keep a list of its members, and under G.S. 55A-16-02 a member may inspect and copy the corporation's records on five business days' written notice (accounting records and similar records require a good-faith, proper-purpose demand that describes the records with reasonable particularity).

Records protected by the attorney-client privilege may generally be withheld, but the statutes do not give a board a general right to refuse inspection because it prefers privacy.

If the association refuses, owners may seek a court order compelling production. For planned communities, G.S. 47F-3-120 lets the court award reasonable attorneys' fees to the prevailing party only if the declaration allows recovery of attorneys' fees; for condominiums, G.S. 47C-4-117 lets the court award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party. Some communities created before 1999 are governed mainly by their original recorded declarations rather than Chapter 47F, so check your community's creation date.
letterStrategy:
A strong North Carolina HOA records demand letter accomplishes three things: it identifies the legal authority, specifies exactly which records you want, and sets a reasonable deadline with consequences for non-compliance.

Start by citing N.C.G.S. § 47F-3-118 (or § 47C-3-118 for condos) and quoting the language requiring records to be "reasonably available." Identify yourself as a lot or unit owner in good standing and list your property address. Then list the specific records requested, such as meeting minutes for specified dates, financial statements for specific fiscal years, the annual income and expense statement and balance sheet, and any contracts or other records you need. The more specific your request, the harder it is for the board to claim confusion.

Set a clear deadline, generally 10 business days, and offer flexibility on format (electronic delivery is often easiest). State that you are willing to pay reasonable copying charges but request an itemized cost estimate before any fees are incurred.

Close by noting that failure to comply will leave you no choice but to seek judicial enforcement, including a court order compelling production and fees and costs where your declaration or the law allows them. Send the letter by certified mail with return receipt to both the HOA's registered agent (searchable on the North Carolina Secretary of State's website) and the management company. Keep copies of everything.

Most boards comply once they see a properly cited demand. The letter signals you understand your rights and are prepared to escalate, which often resolves the dispute without litigation.
proceduralNotes: If the HOA ignores your letter, you have two main options in North Carolina. A small claim action in magistrate's court is limited to $10,000 and to monetary relief, recovery of specific personal property, or summary ejectment (G.S. 7A-210), so a request to compel document production generally belongs in District Court. Be aware that some HOA declarations require pre-suit mediation or arbitration; check your governing documents. Attorney's fees are recoverable only if authorized by statute or contract: G.S. 47F-3-120 allows the court to award fees to the prevailing party in an action to enforce the declaration, bylaws or rules if the declaration allows recovery of fees, and G.S. 47C-4-117 allows a discretionary award in condominium actions.

faq.q: What records can I request from my North Carolina HOA?
faq.a: Under N.C.G.S. § 47F-3-118, you can request the association's financial and other records, including records of meetings of the association and executive board, as required in the bylaws and Chapter 55A, and you are entitled to the annual income and expense statement and balance sheet at no charge within 75 days after fiscal year-end. Under G.S. 55A-16-01 and 55A-16-02, a nonprofit association must also keep and allow member inspection of its articles, bylaws, and recent member meeting minutes and communications on five business days' written notice. Privileged attorney-client communications may be withheld.

faq.q: How quickly must my HOA respond to a records request?
faq.a: North Carolina law requires records to be "reasonably available" but § 47F-3-118 does not specify an exact deadline; if the association is a nonprofit corporation, G.S. 55A-16-02 requires five business days' written notice of an inspection demand. Setting a clear deadline in your demand letter, such as 10 business days, establishes a benchmark for reasonableness. If the HOA delays unreasonably or refuses outright, that delay strengthens any later court action seeking enforcement.

faq.q: Can the HOA charge me for copies of records?
faq.a: Many associations now provide records electronically at no cost.

faq.q: What if my HOA refuses to provide records?
faq.a: If the HOA ignores or denies your written request, you can file suit in North Carolina District Court seeking a court order compelling production. Fees are recoverable only where the declaration allows them (G.S. 47F-3-120) or, for condominiums, in the court's discretion (G.S. 47C-4-117). Before filing, check your governing documents for any required mediation or alternative dispute resolution procedures. Many disputes resolve once a lawsuit is filed, but the records request demand letter is a critical first step that establishes the HOA's non-compliance.

faq.q: Does this apply to older HOAs in North Carolina?
faq.a: The Planned Community Act (Chapter 47F) applies to communities created on or after January 1, 1999, but G.S. 47F-1-102(c) makes certain provisions, including the records provision § 47F-3-118, apply to earlier communities. Condominiums created after October 1, 1986, fall under Chapter 47C, and § 47C-3-118 also applies to earlier condominiums. North Carolina nonprofit corporation law (Chapter 55A, Article 16) provides additional inspection rights for members of nonprofit HOAs.
